item.title: 27 arrests and 248 potential victims identified in action week against labour exploitation
item.description: Europol, the European Labour Authority (ELA), and 34 participating countries today announced the results of an action week targeting human trafficking for labour exploitation. The operation, part of an EMPACT action led by Sweden, brought together police, border guards, labour and social security inspectorates, and tax authorities to crack down on exploitative practices in high-risk sectors such as agriculture, construction, cosmetic services, massage parlours, and hospitality.

item.title: Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: AL26-028 – Ongoing Help Desk Voice Phishing Campaign Targeting Canadian Organizations
67% of security leaders say their teams struggle to meet business needs
item.description:
AI, identity-based attacks, and expanding digital operations are putting pressure on already overstretched cybersecurity teams.

Security vendor Barracuda’s Cybersecurity Skills Gap report also found that security teams are struggling to keep pace with expanding responsibilities. The vast majority of the 2,000 IT and security decision-makers surveyed report cybersecurity skills gaps.

In particular, the most common challenges are linked to AI-related risks (68%) and advanced identity and phishing threats (67%), including business email compromise, OAuth abuse, and multi-factor authentication bypass.

Two-thirds (67%) of respondents say security teams are under pressure and struggling to scale to meet evolving business needs. Half say their security professionals are expected to support growing digital operations without additional resources.

More than half (56%) report a reduction in security head count linked to AI, split evenly between entry-level and more senior roles. As AI takes on more routine analysis and response activities, human roles are shifting toward (higher value) threat investigation, incident leadership, automation governance, and business risk management.

“AI is changing the cybersecurity landscape faster than many security teams can build the necessary skills, visibility, and governance,” said Siroui Mushegian, senior vice president and chief information officer at Barracuda. “Organizations need to reshape their security teams, combining the power of AI and automation with human expertise, judgment, and visibility.”

Hiring challenges

CSO parent company Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities report found that cloud security (35%), securing agentic AI technology (34%), and securing AI/machine learning-enabled technology (30%) topped the areas CSOs felt their teams needed to become more skilled and knowledgeable about in order to meet overall corporate security objectives.

Underlining the difficulty of this ambition, the report found that cloud security architects, AI security specialist, and forensics analysts were the most difficult cybersecurity roles in which to find suitable applicants.

Accessing the cost of the skills gap

Separately, technology-focused online learning platform Pluralsight’s Tech Skills Report 2026 found that 41% of cybersecurity professionals in the UK estimate skills gaps cost them at least £380,000 each year (US$500,000). This estimated cost includes hiring and outsourcing expenses, lost revenue, abandoned projects, and poorly maintained technology.

A quarter of cybersecurity professionals say their organization has experienced security incidents or vulnerabilities over the past 12 months due to skills gaps. Almost half (43%) admitted that skills gaps are a common reason for abandoning cybersecurity projects.

The findings highlight the pressure on security teams as AI adoption increases demand for cybersecurity expertise, Pluralsight concludes.

AI imperative exacerbating skills problem

Europe is short of more than 300,000 cybersecurity professionals, and companies are now struggling to find qualified candidates or applicants, according to research by the AI Workforce Consortium.

Cybersecurity job postings requiring AI skills have doubled year over year across G7 countries. Senior cybersecurity roles requiring AI skills are up 65% year-on-year, compared with 5.9% for junior roles.

The research by the AI Workforce Consortium — an industry group backed by Cisco, Google, Microsoft, IBM, SAP, and others — also points to a growing need for practical experience and human skills.

item.title: UK organisations warned to brace for AI-powered ransomware attacks
item.description:
AI-powered malware is “highly likely” to be used in ransomware attacks on Britain’s critical national infrastructure within the next two years.

The head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre, Dr. Richard Horne, warned that abuse of AI technologies is making it much easier for attackers to rapidly expose and exploit long-neglected security weaknesses.

Dr. Horne argued that underinvestment in technology and security have left organisations carrying a technical debt that leave them wide open to attack.

AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation, the latest edition of the NCSC’s State of the Cyber Nation annual report warns. The issue is more that AI will allow attackers to exploit overlooked vulnerabilities rather than forge exotic new attacks.

The report identifies state-linked threat groups, particularly China and Russia, as the UK’s primary cyber antagonists. For example, in July 2026 the NCSC warned that Russian groups were systematically exploiting vulnerable routers and globally targeting networks maintained by critical national infrastructure providers, including energy grids and telecommunications networks.

In August 2026 the NCSC warned about increased targeting of operational technology systems across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK.

“AI will continue to be integrated into threat actors’ cyber operations, increasing the speed, scale and efficiency of existing attack methodologies rather than autonomously conducting end-to-end attacks,” the NCSC report predicts.

The NCSC reports that up to 88% of all attacks originate from just four vectors: phishing, exploiting public-facing applications, misuse of valid accounts, and exploiting external remote services.

Variations on a theme

“None of these vectors are radical or new,” said Oliver Spence, CEO of security operations tools vendor CybaVerse. “In fact, they represent the same failures cybercriminals have successfully exploited for decades.”

Spence added: “Threat actors rarely depend on the most complex, technical means for launching attacks; more often than not, they search for the most easily exploitable holes in organisations’ systems, like misconfigured VPNs and vulnerabilities in third-party vendor software platforms, and on tried-and-true social engineering techniques.”

AI doesn’t represent a sea-change in attackers’ strategies but rather a force multiplier.

“Threat actors may be able to leverage AI to launch more sophisticated attacks, but the real danger is in the automated exploitation of existing weaknesses and organisational failures,” Spence concluded.

Countermeasures

AI offers a means to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but it will only be effective if organisations deal with years of underinvestment and foundational weaknesses before building from a more solid foundation, according to Dr. Horne.

The UK government’s Cyber Essentials scheme should become the starting point or baseline for enterprise cyber security, not the end goal, for building improved cyber resilience.

Last week the UK government pledged £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, which will be task to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, run by the NCSC.

item.title: A compromised DevOps laptop caused the $6.3B Binance breach
item.description:
Cryptocurrency Exchange Binance blamed a compromised DevOps laptop for the loss of $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency last week, adding that it will now cover any losses faced by its customers.

“Binance will cover all losses from the Secure Assets Fund for Users (SAFU) and the company’s funds,” the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an update on Friday, adding that user funds are safe and that it had found no evidence of wallet private-key leakage during its investigation of the incident. It had frozen approximately $3 billion in assets on-chain, temporarily suspending withdrawals while security checks were completed, and revoking the affected address authorization.

Withdrawals are now being restored in phases, initially reopening services across 15 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and XRP. Binance says it has replenished approximately 95% of the affected assets using company funds, while the remaining 5%, comprising less-liquid tokens, could take longer to source.

The exchange said its preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised employee device that enabled access to a service container involved in withdrawals.

“This attack, reportedly on a development engineer, highlights that security is a critical element of every operational stage and personnel level,” said Tim Rawlins, senior advisor and director of security at NCC Group. “When security failures in trusted identities and administrative access can be targeted, attackers can exploit more than just the underlying technical vulnerabilities.”

The FBI has since attributed the attack to North Korean threat actors, identifying the TraderTraitor hacking group as responsible for the theft.

“Given what we know about the activities of countries like North Korea in targeting cryptocurrency, it’s unsurprising that attackers are prepared to invest considerable efforts in targeting individuals who have access to the building blocks of the exchanges,” Rawlins said.

A compromised laptop reaches the withdrawal pipeline

Binance’s preliminary findings suggest that attackers compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop before gaining access to a service container and submitting unauthorized withdrawals. The exchange has yet to publish technical details of the attack, leaving important questions about the precise intrusion path and how the attackers navigated its internal systems.

“A platform holding digital assets should have multiple layers of security to prevent a single compromise, such as an employee’s laptop being hacked, from being sufficient to authorize a transfer,” said Mario Rivas, blockchain and digital assets security lead at NCC Group.

The reported attack is similar to the February 2025 Bybit breach, in which attackers compromised a developer’s machine at Safe{Wallet} and manipulated the interface presented to transaction signers. However, the Binance incident involved a different mechanism.

F6’s Threat Intelligence Department (TID) said the Binance attack reportedly targeted an automated withdrawal process rather than directly deceiving authorized signers. Evgeniy Yanov, Head of Audit and Consulting Department at F6, cited Crypto security platform Blockaid, highlighting a batch of 50 EIP-7702 authorizations within a single transaction, alongside delegation to a malicious “sweeper” contract, as an unusual feature of the reported attack.

“This specific mechanism has not been seen before in large-scale breaches of this size,” Yanov said.

FBI points to North Korea’s TraderTraitor operation

The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit considered part of the broader Lazarus infrastructure.

The agency, working with the US Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, said it had observed the attackers converting stolen assets privately into Ethereum. It warned that the funds could subsequently be laundered through decentralized finance platforms and instant-swap services.

F6’s TID said the attribution was based on a combination of on-chain and off-chain intelligence. “The group’s signature matches previous thefts: small Tornado Cash withdrawals used to fund the operator’s wallet, extensive preparation well before the actual heist, and pre-signed transactions executed in a single burst,” it added.

TID researchers noted similarities with previous North Korean-linked cryptocurrency thefts, including the Bybit and KelpDAO incidents. However, they cautioned that Binance has not independently named the perpetrators and that the full attribution evidence has not been published.

Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

NCC Group’s Rawlins noted that the growing use of AI could help attackers chain vulnerabilities and operational weaknesses together, while organizations increasingly face adversaries willing to invest considerable effort when the potential financial return is substantial. “Good cyber hygiene and effective security fundamentals are key to defending against attacks that many organizations are still missing,” he said.

item.title: Node-RED authentication hole being exploited in the wild
item.description:
Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild. 

The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday. 

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115, an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.”

The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live. 

Patrick Garrity, the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this. 

“They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview.

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild.

“The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks: equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.”

Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED. 

“It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.”

Another problem is that industrial system patches tend to happen on pre-planned schedules, rather than responding to emergent issues or suggested setting changes.

“Siemens published its advisory on August 11, and VulnCheck caught exploitation on October 30, three days after shipping its own detections,” Mahapatra said. “Eleven weeks is a short runway in OT, where firmware updates wait for planned maintenance windows, so a meaningful share of affected gateways will remain unpatched well into next year.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the details of the exploits are a good news/bad news situation for CISOs. The good news is that the attacks did not appear to have targeted industrial systems. The bad news is the attackers found and accessed those systems anyway.

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, agreed. 

“They don’t necessarily need to understand the equipment or operations connected to these gateways. They’re simply looking for systems capable of executing their commands,” he said. “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place. Even generic malware consuming system resources or interfering with network communications could have operational consequences.”

Dickson added that closing this hole may not resolve the exposure. “The report also found that some attackers skipped the bot and left web shells, hidden back doors for running commands later,” Dickson said. “Patching closes the door. It does not evict anyone already inside.”

item.title: Barracuda’s security appliances have a security problem of their own
item.description:
Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself.

The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices.

They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities.

Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately.

The vulnerabilities impact numerous popular Barracuda products

Root access on an email gateway puts the attacker in the place that every inbound and outbound message passes, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. It may also expose the credentials and connections the gateway uses to reach the mail server and directory. “Those are the keys to the kingdom, if you will,” he said.

CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 both impact Barracuda’s Email Security Gateway (ESG), but CVE-2026-111560 also impacts its Web Security Gateway (WSG), Web Application Firewall (WAF), WAF Control Center (WCC), Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), and Message Archiver (BMA), the company said.

Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches, it advised. The device will show the latest firmware version available; if a device’s firmware is multiple versions out of date, users may need to perform several updates.

Enterprises whose appliances’ admin interfaces are not publicly accessible from the web are less exposed, Barracuda said; the company advised restricting access to these interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls to limit exposure.

“The biggest concern is how these two vulnerabilities could chain together,” said Jon Nelson, principal advisory director at Infotech, noting that an attacker who can bypass authentication and then exploit command injection could move from accessing an exposed appliance to executing commands on it. “Assessing each vulnerability in isolation can understate the risk,” he said.

Dickson added that security leaders should read the advisory closely, as it calls one flaw “pre-authentication,” then lists “Authentication Required: Yes, administrative access.”

“Both cannot be true in the usual sense,” he pointed out. Likely access here means being able to reach the admin interface over the network, without a password.

“If your admin interface faces the internet, that condition is already met,” Dickson said.

The advisory also labels a 9.3 severity rating as “high,” when 9.0 and above is actually “critical” on the standard scale, he pointed out. “These are small things, but labels drive patching queues,” he noted. Also, the advisory does not say whether these flaws are currently being exploited, but it does not say they are not, either.

How enterprises should respond

“Get the admin interface off the internet,” Dickson emphasized, noting that, as a cybersecurity consultant, he gives that advice at least a handful of times a week. “Management interfaces on edge devices are continually a source of vulnerability.”

Once teams limit admin access to a trusted internal network or a dedicated management network, Dickson advised, they should then “verify the patch rather than assume it was properly installed.” From there, he said, analyze for unauthorized visitors by reviewing admin logs, check for unfamiliar accounts, and look for unexpected outbound connections from the device.

History matters here, he added. In 2023, after a zero-day on this same email security gateway (ESG), Barracuda told customers with compromised appliances to replace them outright rather than rely on the patch. As he put it: “A patch fixes the lock. It does not tell you who already has a key.”

Nelson agreed that enterprises should look closely at who can reach their administrative interfaces. They should, in addition, put access behind additional controls such as a properly configured zero trust access layer.

“Exposing those interfaces directly to the internet was always a bad idea,” he said. “As AI makes it easier to find weaknesses and chain attacks together, that exposure becomes increasingly difficult to justify.” AI is also expanding the search for software flaws to include issues such as business logic weaknesses where an application can be made to bypass its intended controls. Authentication and authorization bypasses deserve particular attention in that context, Nelson said.

As more vendors use advanced AI to examine their code, CISOs should prepare for more flaw disclosures and potentially shorter windows to respond to them, he noted. “That means identifying exposed appliances, restricting access, and having a response plan ready before the next zero day arrives,” he said.

Understanding what each appliance exposes

Security appliances are increasingly creating vulnerabilities in corporate networks, which is changing the cybersecurity discussion. Enterprises rely on them to protect the network, yet ultimately they are software systems with vulnerabilities of their own.

“They sit exactly where attackers want to be,” Dickson noted.

Firewalls, VPNs, and email gateways face the internet by design; that is their job, he said. They see sensitive traffic and hold credentials. Most cannot run the endpoint detection tools that protect laptops and servers, so a compromise can remain undetected for a long time, and every customer runs the same firmware, so one working exploit can scale to thousands of organizations.

“The discussion is shifting from which box to buy to what the box itself exposes,” Dickson said. “Every appliance purchase is a decision to trust a vendor’s code at the most exposed point in the network.” It deserves the same scrutiny as any other in an enterprise, he noted.

Buyers should ask their vendors four questions, he advised: Is the admin interface exposed to the internet by default; how quickly do patches ship; are they applied automatically; and what logging can users see?

“The security appliance does not just protect the perimeter,” Dickson pointed out. “It is the perimeter, and it should be treated as the most attacked system an organization owns, because it is.”

item.title: AL26-026 - Critical vulnerabilities impacting PHP - CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 - Update 2
CrowdStrike’s AI SOC vision evolves as agentic uncertainty adds new twist
item.description:
“The software we use has become an actor,” declared CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas in his address on the dangers and opportunity of agentic AI at the company’s Fal.Con conference in September. It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given.

For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this. Agents still work on behalf of humans, but they don’t always reason or act like them. They are entities with capabilities and an unpredictability unlike any threat businesses have ever faced.

“I believe we just crossed a line. Agents have escaped evaluation environments and compromised infrastructure they were never supposed to touch,” Sentonas told the crowd in Las Vegas in early September. “For decades, software did what we programmed it to. It has moved from execution to agency.”

Sentonas’ point wasn’t simply that malicious agents are a threat. The arrival of agentic AI also raises larger questions for security operations centers (SOCs), which will deploy agents on a scale that matches or even exceeds attackers. That makes agents a threat from both the outside and inside the enterprise perimeter. “What happens when millions of AI agents act at machine speed on both sides?” Behind the confident marketing pitches from CrowdStrike and a growing cast of rivals, the honest answer right now is that nobody can be sure.

Coming from a cyber vendor, Sentonas’ reference to “millions” of agents might sound like a number meant to hype the threat. But it is likely no exaggeration, with Gartner forecasting that the number of agents used inside a single Fortune 500 company will expand from 15 in 2025 to 150,000 by 2028.

“As CIOs and IT leaders see an explosion of AI agents across their organizations, many are contending with an ungoverned sprawl of agents that expose their organizations to a range of risks, including misinformation, oversharing, and data loss,” says Matt Goss, a senior director analyst at Gartner.

Taking up the agent challenge

For years, Fal.Con was about persuading enterprise SOCs to consolidate capabilities under CrowdStrike’s do-it-all Falcon platform, comprising nearly three dozen modules. In 2023, with its “Raptor” release, Falcon and the company’s flagship event took a hard turn toward AI. In this changed world, AI wasn’t simply a Falcon capability; increasingly it was Falcon, influencing everything it did.

The AI theme dominated Falcon’s 2026 Fall release, bringing the company’s growing portfolio of AI SOC capabilities under the Falcon umbrella with the launch of the Agentic Security Platform. Most individual components — Charlotte AI AgentWorks, Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration, the AI-enabled Enterprise Graph — were announced in 2025 as part of the company’s Agentic Security Workforce plan but a closer look reveals important new features.

Currently, agents investigate alerts using pre-built Falcon agents or custom agents built using the no-code AgentWorks solution. Charlotte AI now gives these agents a shared memory layer in Enterprise Graph that enables them to coordinate with one another across multiple endpoints, identities, and cloud services simultaneously (aided by the company’s 2025 acquisition of Onum, which accelerated the speed with which agents can ingest data). On paper, the effect is to dramatically speed up alert triage while expanding the scope and capacity of worker agents in a way that relieves human SOC teams of a lot of basic grunt work, including some Level 2 investigation and Level 3 remediation and hunting workflows.

Also new is SafeMind, a frontier red-teaming system based on Nvidia’s Nemotron open-weight LLM, comprising offense (Red Tempest) and defense (Blue Solano). This agentic framework continuously tests an isolated mirror of the live environment for weaknesses, feeding the results back into detection at the agent level. CrowdStrike didn’t invent the concept, but it does appear to be the first to integrate an autonomous testing model into a SOC platform.

Speed is not enough

This might look brand new, but the early incarnations of the agent-powered SOC are as much evolution as revolution. Everything inside a traditional CrowdStrike-powered SOC — from its Falcon EDR sensor, Enterprise Graph data, and cloud-native management — remains in place. Humans are still essential to decision-making, albeit at a higher level than before. What agents add to this SOC paradigm is a new abstraction layer separating SOC teams from the mass of telemetry they have increasingly struggled with. This should be good news for defenders because it means they have some hope of matching the speed and scale of agentic attacks.

But speed is only the beginning, points out James Patrick, CTO for the FIOR Group, which develops an AI policy and security gateway. “Attackers and defenders can both operate at machine speed, so simply making SOCs faster isn’t enough. We need to move beyond reactive detection towards continuous testing of our defenses.”

SOCs must work out how much they delegate to agents and what constraints are set around this. “Enterprises already struggle with fragmented telemetry, overlapping security products and inconsistent policies. Adding autonomous systems introduces another problem: establishing who or what has authority to act, and how to verify that authority,” says Patrick.

According to Chris Cochran, field CISO and VP of AI security for the SANS Institute, that’s why “for most organizations, agentic AI will be augmentative rather than a replacement for analysts, at least for the next few years.”

Agent platforms, including CrowdStrike’s, still have work to do proving themselves in terms of oversight and governance.

“The core problem is that we’re applying a probabilistic technology to a discipline that usually requires determinism,” Cochran adds. “A SOC needs to know that the same input will produce the same action, and that the action can be explained to an auditor or an incident review board.”

For that reason, Cochran believes that while agentic-powered SOCs will remove a huge amount of alert handling and correlation effort, the workload will shift to processes such as verification.

“Teams should continuously evaluate agents against known-good and known-bad cases, the same way you’d regression test detection content,” he says. “None of this is exotic, but it takes engineering time that many SOCs haven’t budgeted for.”

Enemy within

One deeply unfamiliar problem is that agents themselves are an emerging attack surface within the enterprise and must be constantly assessed. Traditionally, security tools defend the environment, and the idea that an agent system doing the same job could itself become a direct threat is new. But what makes agentic AI unsettlingly is its non-deterministic nature, which means that, unlike a traditional security tool, it has the potential to do things you didn’t tell it to and haven’t planned for.

“Organizations are deploying autonomous systems that access sensitive data, use privileged identities, interact with applications, and execute actions. Those agents can be compromised, manipulated, or behave unexpectedly,” says Tom Findling, CEO and cofounder at AI SOC startup Conifers.ai. “Security operations will need visibility into agent identities, permissions, actions, and decision-making processes, and the ability to detect and contain dangerous behavior.”

CrowdStrike’s answer, relaunched at this year’s Fal.Con, is Falcon Guardian, an AI detection and response (AIDR) solution featuring runtime enforcement, agent discovery, execution graph mapping prompts, and quarantining for misbehaving agents. Similar capabilities will be needed for any agent platform but the mere fact that security systems now need their own security systems underscores what CrowdStrike’s Sentonas was referring to with his software-as-actor remark at Fal.Con. Human SOCs need to protect their enterprises from their AI SOC helpers.

To that end, CrowdStrike yesterday announced the roughly $400 million acquisition of Fiddler AI, an AI agent monitoring and governance vendor from the emerging, burgeoning, and somewhat confusing agentic AI tools ecosystem.

Fiddler’s platform tracks AI models’ behavior, attempting to provide explanations for their actions as a means for establishing a control plane for governing and securing them. Its 100-plus metrics track hallucinations, toxicity, personally identifiable information (PII) leakage, and drift, enforcing policies to protect against jailbreaks, prompt injections, and bias. Enterprises deploy tools like Fiddler to make model drift visible and actionable before it becomes systemic risk.

CrowdStrike intends to bundle Fiddler into its flagship platform as Falcon Observe in Q4 FY2027, approximately six months from now, as a means for “proving businesses can safely use AI agents every day,” according to Sentonas’ post announcing the acquisition.

CrowdStrike has invested heavily in agentic AI, building an impressive stack of capabilities that extend the Enterprise Graph that made it a dominant player capable of surviving the occasional embarrassing global hiccup. It has even embraced a degree of openness, allowing data ingestion, API connectors, and partnership gateways to enrich the data going into its Falcon AIDR. However, there’s no getting away from Falcon as the single control plane.

“CrowdStrike starts with endpoint security and an established enterprise security platform. Other vendors approach the problem through identity, networks, cloud, or security analytics. They all have an incentive to bring customers further into their own platforms,” observes FIOR Group’s Patrick.

“The challenge for CrowdStrike, and for every vendor, is that a platform can’t independently verify itself,” he adds. “What’s needed is control that is genuinely independent of any single platform and works across those boundaries.”

According to Patrick, a critical feature will be the ability not simply to deploy a security layer but to continuously assess its security and performance. As the traditional detection and remediation stack of cybersecurity is pushed out of shape, the growth in new layers and processes could make this task almost as demanding as the main job of cyber defense that agents were supposed to simplify.

item.title: AL26-027 - Critical vulnerability impacting Google Brotli – CVE-2026-111497
CrowdStrike to acquire Fiddler, Dreadnode to extend AI security across agent lifecycle
item.description:
CrowdStrike plans to acquire AI security companies Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in separate deals that will extend its Falcon platform into automated testing of AI systems and monitoring of AI agent behaviour, as enterprises look to address security risks arising from increasingly autonomous applications.

CrowdStrike made the announcements at Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona, saying the acquisitions will add capabilities to test AI models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment and monitor their decisions and actions in production.

The company plans to integrate Dreadnode’s automated testing technology and Fiddler’s agent observability capabilities into Falcon, with both offerings scheduled for general availability in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.

Dreadnode will bring automated security testing to identify vulnerabilities in AI models, applications and agents before deployment. Fiddler, meanwhile, will add AI agent observability and explainability, allowing enterprises to monitor agent behaviour, trace decisions and understand why agents take particular actions, CrowdStrike said in two separate statements.

CrowdStrike said the Dreadnode team will join its Cyber Superintelligence Lab, but did not specify how the Fiddler team would be integrated into the company.

CrowdStrike adds AI testing and observability

“With this acquisition, Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform into the layer where enterprises build and test AI, delivering Automated AI Security Testing capabilities,” CrowdStrike said in its announcement.

It further added that Dreadnode’s technology will allow security teams to test AI models, applications, agent reasoning loops and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers against more than 100 AI attack strategies. These include jailbreaks, prompt injection, multi-turn attacks, and attacks targeting AI agents.

The technology will also let teams describe tests in natural language, rank findings by severity, and map vulnerabilities to frameworks including OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, OWASP Agentic Security, MITRE ATLAS, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. CrowdStrike said findings will feed into Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations.

Fiddler, the second acquisition, will bring agent observability and explainability capabilities to Falcon. CrowdStrike said the technology is intended to address risks that can arise even when agents have not been compromised.

“An agent can hold valid credentials and approved tools and still make unsupported decisions, ignore instructions, or claim work it never completed. They don’t have to be compromised to create risk,” the company said in a statement.

CrowdStrike plans to offer Fiddler’s technology through Falcon Observe. The product will evaluate agent accuracy, task completion, and policy compliance before deployment, and trace decisions, reasoning paths, and tool calls once agents are in production, the company said.

The company further added that Falcon Observe will also detect behavioural drift, hallucinations and unintended actions, while maintaining records of agent activity for compliance and audit purposes. The offering is expected to support OpenTelemetry and frameworks including LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Strands and Google ADK, it added.

Governance remains a shared responsibility

The addition of observability and automated testing to a security platform could help enterprises correlate agent behaviour with identity, runtime activity and security events, said Apeksha Kaushik, senior principal analyst at Gartner.

However, Kaushik said the acquisitions would not make security teams the sole owners of AI agent governance. Platform and observability teams would continue to be responsible for reliability, performance and operational telemetry, while application security and AI teams would retain responsibility for secure development and testing.

“Business, data and compliance leaders also retain accountability for use cases, data and regulatory obligations,” Kaushik said.

She said CIOs should establish a governance model that defines responsibilities across engineering, security, risk, and business teams. CISOs, meanwhile, should ensure security teams have the authority to set minimum controls, monitor agent behaviour and intervene when activity creates unacceptable risk.

Integration and roadmap questions

CrowdStrike expects both transactions to close during its fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, and has scheduled both offerings for general availability in the same quarter.

Kaushik cautioned enterprises against treating the announced timelines as confirmation of final product capabilities or integration plans.

“Enterprises should distinguish between announced plans and demonstrated product capability, with closing timeline and conditions possibly being different, especially with the pace of change of the threat landscape and evolution of AI,” she added.

She advised customers to seek clarity on pricing, packaging, migration terms, service continuity, support commitments, deployment models, data handling, telemetry retention and API access.

“Once the Existing and prospective customers have further details, they should set up their roadmap changes, support commitments, service continuity, contract and pricing, data portability, open integrations, and access to historical data changes,” she pointed out. CrowdStrike did not disclose the financial terms of either acquisition.
